newsitem.title: PERU: Four Peruvian officers arrested in torture case.
newsitem.headline: Four Peruvian officers arrested in torture case.

text.p: Police on Wednesday arrested four Peruvian army officers accused of torturing an intelligence agent whom they suspected of leaking information to the press, a military spokesman said.

The arrests of Col. Carlos Sanchez and three other officers were the first in a growing scandal in Peru over abuses committed against two women agents alleged to have passed information to the media. One of the agents was killed.
"All four have been arrested in line with the orders from the military judge," said the spokesman. They were being held in a Lima army base awaiting questioning.
A military prosecutor charged the four on Tuesday with abuse of authority in the torture of Leonor La Rosa, a non- commissioned army intelligence officer now recovering from severe burns and lesions.

La Rosa said in a television interview from her hospital room on Sunday that she had learned of a campaign by rogue army officers to intimidate opponents of President Alberto Fujimori. The four officers suspected her, mistakenly, of leaking information about the plan, and beat and tortured her, she said.
Fujimori has denied there was any such plan.
La Rosa herself faces charges -- for insubordination and breach of secrecy for granting the TV interview.
In a related and potentially more explosive case, an army intelligence agent and friend of La Rosa, Mariella Barreto, was found murdered and savagely mutilated on Easter on Sunday.

Another TV report, citing unidentified sources, said Barreto had been accused by other agents of leaking information to the media about the killings of nine university students and their professor in 1992.
The massacre, known as the La Cantuta case, shocked Peruvians and led to convictions of six army officers -- all later pardoned by a Congress dominated by Fujimori supporters.
None of the four men arrested in La Rosa's case has been charged with the murder of Barreto, whose body was found by a shepherd, with its hands and head missing, in a field outside Lima.

Both cases have dominated Peruvian headlines while Fujimori has grappled with the siege of the Japanese ambassador's home by Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages. One of the captives is the congressman who drafted the law granting pardons in La Cantuta case.

At a special session of Congress on Wednesday, legislators blasted the army and government over the two cases and some demanded the resignations of Defence Minister Tomas Castillo and Interior Minister Juan Briones.
